These estimates of revenue and expenditure indicate an estimated deficit for the current year of approximately $23,000,000. I do not think it will be larger than this. It may indeed be substantially smaller, if the west produces a good crop, if the business trend in the United States and other important countries is reversed at an early date, and if our own construction industry takes full advantage of the opportunities now afforded to it. I may add that the results of such favourable developments will not be wholly realized until next year and not be fully reflected in the government accounts until the next budget.
In view of the current business situation, we have not thought it wise to attempt this year to wipe out a possible deficit of the moderate proportions I have indicated by imposing further burdens upon industry and upon the people. On the contrary in the tax changes which are being proposed we are trying in the first place to eliminate certain

anomalies and inequities and in the second place to make certain important adjustments designed to accelerate the forces making for business recovery.
Tax Changes
Under the Income War Tax Act, no changes will be made in the rates of tax on individual and corporate incomes. Amendments to this act, however, will include a provision to allow Canadian companies a deduction in respect of lump sum contributions to employees' pension funds covering past years' services, such deductions to be spread forward over a ten-year period. The government hopes that this concession will encourage the present tendency in industry to create pension funds for employees. Annuities received under the provisions of any will or trust will be made taxable. In respect of royalties paid abroad from sources within Canada, no deduction will be allowed on account of the amount of any such royalties passed on to another party. An amendment will also be made to assure that financial companies operating in the small loan field will in future be subject in all cases to the normal corporation tax rates. The gift tax provisions are to be amended in order to allow an exemption up to one-half of a person's taxable income less the amount of income tax paid. This is to meet the objection which has been raised in this house to the fact that the gift tax in its present form is unduly severe in its effects on gifts which were not made for the purpose of tax avoidance. At the same time, we propose to discourage still further the making of gifts for tax avoidance purposes by substantially increasing the rates applying to gifts in excess of the increased exemption. The new schedule of rates will be graduated from 5 per cent on gifts totalling $25,000 or less, up to 15 per cent on gifts of $1,000,000 and over.
Provision is also to be made to allow Canadian parent companies an exemption from corporation tax in respect of dividends received from wholly-owned non-resident subsidiaries if at least 75 per cent of the combined capital of the parent and subsidiary companies is employed abroad and if the country in which the subsidiary is located grants a like exemption to parent companies in respect of subsidiaries in Canada.
It is also proposed to insert a provision in the act designed to prevent taxpayers from effecting transactions, using persons or corporations abroad for the purpose of evading Canadian taxation and not for business reasons.

The Budget-Mr. Dunning
No changes are proposed in respect of rates of tax under the Excise Act.
Under the Special War Revenue Act, one important change and several minor ones are proposed. The minor changes, include an amendment to exempt from the sales tax feed for all fur bearing animals, harness, harness parts and materials used in the manufacture thereof, ingredients used in making gopher poison, and materials for the repair of fishermen's boats. Another amendment provides that in future the special excise tax on tires and tubes will in no case be levied when the items in question are for original equipment of automotive vehicles including tractors, trucks, trailers and motor cycles.
I come now to the most important change in taxation which the government proposes. Starting to-morrow the major products used for the building of houses, will be given complete exemption from sales tax. It is proposed that this exemption from sales tax shall cover all lumber, sashes, doors, laths, and shingles; bricks, building tile, building blocks, cement, stone, plaster and lime; plaster boards, fibre board, insulating materials, building paper and wallpaper; paints, varnishes, white lead and paint oil; prepared roofings; glass for buildings; plumbing fixtures, not including piping and pipe fittings; furnaces for heating buildings; builders' hardware; and some other minor items. It will be realized, I am sure, that an exemption of the type here attempted presents considerable difficulties, and it was found impossible to provide specific exemption in respect of all the hundreds of various miscellaneous items entering into the construction of houses. It was necessary to make a selection but all the important materials which have their primary or predominant use in house-building are included. Accordingly, lumber, for example, although having many other uses, will be tax-exempt no matter for what purpose it is used. This will be the case with all the items exempted.
I believe the house will agree that this proposed tax change is highly constructive. Coupled with the various legislative measures which the government has already introduced, this tax reduction should act as a further powerful stimulus to the construction industry. If these various measures now before the house result in restoring normal construction activity, a large proportion of our remaining employable unemployed will go back on the payrolls of industry and to self-reliant citizenship. These important objectives are in my opinion ample justification for so radical a proposal. I need only add that the benefits of these tax reductions must be passed on to the consumer, and personally I am confident
that the construction industry, for which so much is being done, will rise to the occasion with a renewed efficiency and vigour worthy of the great opportunity now presented to it.

For reasons which I believe will commend themselves to the house, I am not proposing any amendments to the customs tariff in the present budget resolutions. It is true that the government had hoped that it would be found feasible to deal with a new United States agreement as part of this year's budget. Circumstances, however, have compelled us to abandon that expectation and the government, therefore, is not proposing any changes in the Canadian tariff pending the satisfactory conclusion of the negotiations now in progress.
In the budget speech two years ago, I said, "Canada cannot give to-day and bargain to-morrow." It is even, more true, Mr. Speaker, in the world as it is to-day that unilateral tariff reductions will not get the wider export markets which our products need and which the government is securing for them. Since the present administration came into office, Canada has been a contracting party to the two most comprehensive trade agreements that have been concluded since the great war. Our agreement with the United States in 1935 and our agreement with the United Kingdom in 1937 resulted in the reduction of effective duties on a wide range of Canadian imports. They also secured the enlargement and consolidation of marketing opportunities for Canadian exports in the two biggest import markets of the world, which in the last calendar year took between them about eighty per cent of Canada's total exports. They were long strides towards our goal-both in intra-imperial and international trade-of lowering tariff barriers and freeing trade from fettering restrictions. We are now ready for further progress in this direction and we hope to take it in concert with the United Kingdom and the United States.
No commercial treaty policy can, in the nature of things, ensure against the disturbing influences on our national economy of industrial depression to the south of us, or of wars and rumours of wars to the east and the west of us. These disturbing influences are apparent from the most casual scrutiny of our trade returns. The returns reveal an expansion of those exports for which demand has been increased by the fears of war, and at the same time a falling off in the value of those exports for which demand depends on peace and prosperity in the countries which normally buy our goods. This is not, fundamentally, a healthy condition. The
The Budget-Mr. Dunning

world itself is not in a healthy condition and Canada's economic relations with the outside world reflect the disturbances beyond our frontiers.
I see no reasonable hope of restoring normal trade relations except by a vigorous prosecution of the policy of tariff reduction through bilateral trade agreements, a policy for which this government has stood since its entry into office. For better or worse, the force of circumstances has eliminated at least for the present the alternative approaches of unilateral or universal action. The United States is not prepared to reduce its tariffs except by way of trade agreements, and the United Kingdom is now pursuing a similar policy. This being the present attitude of our two best customers, it is surely apparent that Canada should try to reach agreement with them rather than to pursue at this time an isolated policy of further unilateral tariff reductions. I do not think there should be any real difference of opinion as to where the national interest of this country lies. It is bound up inseparably with the restoration of free and stable international trading conditions. Every effort in that direction has had and will continue to have our wholehearted support and practical cooperation.
It would not be proper for me, at this time, to make any statement with regard to the negotiations looking toward the conclusion of new trade agreements between Canada and the United States, and the United States and the United Kingdom, which have been pursued steadily in Washington for some months now. We have embarked, it is true, on a big and difficult undertaking which for its successful completion will require the continuing collaboration in good faith of all the countries concerned. We believe that all the benefits of the good neighbourhood which we in Canada appreciate in our relations with the United States of America can be fully realized only through closer cooperation in the economic field between the United States and all the countries of the British commonwealth. The process of translating these hopes, which we all share, into concrete results has been difficult and protracted. In the present instance, it is clear that if we are to find fair and practicable solutions to the problems involved. Canada must make its contribution along with the rest towards a general settlement. It is perhaps true that in some areas and in some industries we have been enjoying the best of both worlds, and it has been argued, therefore, that our interest is to sit tight and exploit such privileges for what they are worth-while they last. Such an attitude is obviously shortsighted; it is

certainly not the policy of this government, which is striving, on the basis of reciprocity and fair dealing, to work out trade arrangements with all nations which will serve the best interests of Canada as a whole.
I shall not attempt to prophesy the consequences that may follow from a successful completion of the present negotiations. I cannot refrain, however, from reminding the house that proof of the will and capacity of the countries of the British commonwealth of nations and the United States of America to cooperate in the field of trade will be a political fact of world importance. Conversely, the acknowledgment of inability to do so would limit the influence of the great democracies as a stabilizing factor in a disturbed world. The economic benefits of success in our efforts would not be confined to the trade and prosperity of the countries directly engaged in these negotiations. They would, through the application of the policy of equal treatment in commercial matters, be shared in some degree by every country in the world. The progressive reduction of the tariffs of the great trading nations will undoubtedly lessen the present strains under which the economies of many less fortunate nations are labouring. It should help to turn the nations of the world away from economic nationalism which is both a cause and a consequence of the growing fear of war.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I do not exaggerate when I say that the fate of civilization to-day depends on whether the qualities of toleration, of good-will, of friendly cooperation, of ability to take the far-sighted view and of willingness to sink differences of lesser importance for the sake of the larger interest triumph in human affairs. If I may say so, these old-fashioned qualities are needed not only in international affairs but in the day to day relations between individuals, social groups and political bodies in this country. In spite of all our difficulties, I am confident that the Canadian people possess these qualities to a degree which will ensure continuous and progressive development of a united Canada.

That is what I said, and I repeat it. I hold the return in my hand. In view of the fact that the rules say that one cannot attribute motives to any hon. member, what is the point of order that is well taken?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have given my ruling.
What is it? I do not know, nor does anybody else.

What
was the complaint in the first instance in regard to the return?

I merely recite the fact; that is all. Whereupon a member of this chamber suggests that someone is inferring something. I am not inferring anything at all. speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Let us understand it then.

And the highways to which reference is made are the Piney highway, the Sprague-Morden highway, and the Brandon-Clear Lake highway in Manitoba. Those highways have in part been completed since this government came into office, and the file contains papers with respect to them. But the motion is limited to October 15, 1935.
Subject to agreement we found when we came into office.
Certainly. I am bound to say that I have not been able to see the original file; that is in the possession of the hon. member for Proveneher.
I rise to a point of order.
Another point of order.
The right hon. gentleman has no right to impute motives to any member of the house, or to say things that are untrue. I have not the file in my office.

I inquired of the office downstairs for the original file. I asked to see it just before coming in here to-night, and I was told it had not been returned, that the hon. member for Proveneher (Mr. Beaubien), had it. Perhaps that statement was an error. I am stating the facts only as told me by the officials. I have what purports to be a copy. That is all I have been able to see up to the moment.
I have just sent one of the page boys dowmstairs for the file itself. As soon as I get it I shall send it to my right hon. friend.
If my hon. friend is able to send for it, he must have control over it. The official of the house in charge of the office told me within the last twenty minutes that he had not the file.
The file was produced as an official document of this house and any hon. member can see it.
The hon. member for Proveneher borrowed it.
Anyone can borrow it.

It had not been returned. I went downstairs to the office last week and I could not see it. I called to-night for it and it had not yet been returned. The Secretary of State circulated the order among the various departments. First of all, it went to the Minister of Public Works, and the reply was that there was nothing in the public works department. It then went to the Prime Minister's office and the reply was:
There is nothing on the files of the Prime Minister's office regarding this matter.
Edward A. Pickering,
Assistant Private Secretary.
Then we have the Department of Labour. I am going to place upon the record the story as it appears on this file. On July 23, 1935, the minister of public works and labour of Manitoba sent the following letter:
Department of Public Works and Labour Minister's Office Winnipeg,
23rd July, 1935.
Hon. W. A. Gordon,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Gordon: -
A large delegation interviewed the honourable premier and myself this morning in reference to the construction of a road, as a relief project, from a point four miles east of the town of Morden, thence easterly through the towns of Plum Coulee, Letellier, Dominion City, Stuartburn, Vita, Caliento, Sundown, Menisino and Piney, to the town of Sprague, an approximate distance of 115 miles.
Roughly estimated, this road will cost around $10,000 per mile, plus the construction of a bridge over the Red river at Letellier, which will cost in the neighbourhood of $125,000.
The delegates were very desirous of having this road constructed as an unemployment relief measure, and intimated that the dominion government would favourably consider same.
If you are prepared to do this as a relief measure, the province will undertake to do its part.
Yours very truly,
W. R. Clubb, Minister of Public Works and Labour

Dear Mr. Gordon:
Last month when I was at Ottawa discussing relief projects that might be undertaken in this province, I submitted to Mr. Dickson, deputy minister, a list of same and in which was included the project known as the Piney highway.
This road was started in 1930 as a relief project and considerable work was done in that year and continued in 1931.
The list referred to above, I understand, Mr. Dickson referred to you but in your letter of June 27 you stated that you could not see your way clear to approve of any of this work other than that on the Trans-Canada highway and the Peace Garden road.
Since my return, I have had numerous requests asking me to again take up with you the matter of the completion of the Piney highway and to ask if you would be prepared to reconsider your previous decision.
This highway begins at the city of St. Boniface and runs in a southeasterly direction through the towns of Grande Pointe, Isle de Chene, Steinbach, La Broquerie and Piney and then five miles south to the international boundary, an estimated distance of ninety miles.
The estimated cost of this work is ten thousand dollars per mile less the forty miles which have already been graded.
I would appreciate it if you would let me hear from you in this regard.
Yours very truly,
W. R. Clubb,
Minister of Public Works and Labour.

Dear Mr. Gordon:
I would appreciate it very much indeed, if you would kindly read the enclosed carefully. There is not the question of a doubt but that if we do not do something, many hundreds and thousands of these people in these districts will be applying to the provincial and federal governments for assistance this winter.

That is the next letter on the file. Attached to that is a letter marked "private and personal," written by Mr. Webb to Mr. Bennett. Copies are said to have been sent to the Honourable Wesley A. Gordon, K.C., M.P.; the Honourable J. Earl Lawson, K.C., M.P.; and the Honourable Doctor R. J. Manion, M.P. This letter is dated August 23, 1935, and reads:
The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett,

Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Canada.
My dear Chief:
I have just come in from the constituencies of Lisgar, Provencher and St. Boniface particularly, and the situation at the moment is very good there politically, but it needs the necessary impetus to carry on.
I have already written to the Hon. J. E. Lawson, the Hon. R. J. Manion and the Hon. Wesley Gordon and the Hon. T. G. Murphy with regard to the two roads in these three constituencies that are vital factors to this election campaign, and they have the whole story in detail, both verbally and in writing.
In 1931 the federal government appropriated moneys for both of these roads. Both trunk highways enter the province of Manitoba, and as an unemployment relief measure, quite considerable work was done, which I think was shared by the federal and provincial governments fifty per cent each. The provincial government have or did apply again for these two roads to be carried on as an unemployment relief measure, but for some reason or other were more or less turned down as a matter of policy.
A new problem has arisen lately, which may be a good reason for reconsideration. As you know rust and extreme heat have destroyed the larger portion of our Manitoba wheat crop, and in some parts of Lisgar and Provencher especially it has created a very serious problem, and has left the farmers in a serious situation. My thought is that if your government will cooperate with the provincial government as an unemployment relief works measure,

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
that work could be done on these roads that would give the farmers of these three constituencies plenty to do and help them to earn something, whereas if it is not done they possibly may appeal to the provincial and federal governments for some form of relief and for which we will get nothing, but on the other hand are perfectly willing to work themselves and use their teams and equipment. As a political measure, it assures us without any question of a doubt these three seats which we badly want to win, and which look very good for us at the present time.
Hear, hear.

There will not be so
much "hear, hear" when I finish. The letter continues:
The Liberal federal members in these three constituencies, supported to some extent, under cover, by provincial government members are endeavouring to blame the federal government for the fact that these two roads have not and will not be built, and it has become such a strong factor politically, that a great deal rests on a favourable decision being made.
May I intervene here to point out that according to the record the Liberal candidates in those constituencies were urging that these roads should be built and complaining that the federal government was not providing the means to have them built. That is the position at the moment.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Read the next paragraph.

The letter continues:
I feel that we should play the game politically, call the provincial government's bluff, who have stated positively to delegates that they are prepared to put up dollar for dollar with the federal government in the building of these two roads as an unemployment relief works measure, and I understand, although I am not sure, that the provincial government have forwarded on letters of approval for both of these roads. They certainly did in their original letter of March or April 27, because I have a copy of it, and it was discussed at Ottawa with the Minister of Labour and the Hon. T. G. Murphy.
If the federal government would advise of participation in these two roads, it would be good politics; it would call the provincial government's bluff; it would kill the propaganda that the Liberals are carrying on at the present time; it would assure us of a victory in these three seats, and in my humble opinion, will not have cost the federal government anything, because by the time the work is organized, the election will be over, and winter will be upon us, and perhaps very little work will have been done before the end of the present financial year.
I am not for one moment endeavouring to justify that language. I did not write the letter. If I had written it-

The letter proceeds:
The Hon. W. Gordon, the Hon. Dr. R. J. Manion and the Hon. T. G. Murphy know all about these two roads. They 'have the details, map locations and I believe thoroughly understand the situation. Our candidates are very alive to the situation, and no doubt have also been in touch with your own good self and the ministers, pointing out the actual situation and what it means. If it was not the right thing to do I would be the first to turn it down, but they are essential to the welfare of the province as a whole, running through two very thickly settled parts of the province, in fact the oldest settled parts, and there is not a road anywhere east of the Red river other than mud roads, and the people there are naturally aroused. I am not saying that it is a federal matter at all. we all know that, but as an unemployment relief works measure it is thought that something might be done, and particularly in view of the serious situation that has developed through rust and extreme heat in the crops of the farmers, and politically it means victory for us.
Yours very truly,
R. H. Webb,
Director for Manitoba.
Might I ask the right hon. gentleman what Mr. Webb is director of?
I had not known him by that title until I heard it stated the other day. But it was stated then that he was director of the Conservative organisation in Manitoba.
He is not personally the director of the road work?

Oh, no, he is mayor of Winnipeg and was actively interested in politics.

Dear Mr. Dickson,-
I have received a telegram from the Minister of the Interior reading as follows:
" Regarding further works in the province of Manitoba which might be commenced for the relief of unemployment the following should I feel receive serious consideration: Construction of a highway leading south easterly from Winnipeg to the international boundary known as the Piney highway; construction of a highway from Morden eastward to connect with the Piney highway; construction of a highway from Russeli to a point near Erickson to connect with the highway leading to the Riding Mountain park; construction of a bridge known as the Lens bridge Swan river district. It was asked why that should be sent to the deputy minister and not to the minister. The answer appears in Mr. Clubb's letter to the minister. He said that he left his papers in regard to this matter with Mr. Dickson, because, the minister being absent, it was the custom to leave these matters with Mr. Dickson so that the minister would unquestionably receive them on his return.
May I ask a question?

No. The next letter, which is dated September 4, 1935, reads:
Department of Public Works and Labour Minister's Office,
Winnipeg,
September 4, 1935.
Hon. W. A. Gordon,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Gordon,-
Yesterday Senator Mullins, Mr. R. Peden. of Rossburn. and the Hon. Mr. Griffiths interviewed me with reference to the proposed gravelling of the road from Russell to Clear Lake via Silverton, Angusville, Birdtail, Rossburn, Olha, Oakburn, Menzie, Elphinstone, Sandy Lake and Raclcham to Clear Lake highway.
This road, Mr. Peden informed me, had been approved by the parties interested at a meeting which he had attended. In discussing this matter Mr. Peden also informed me that Senator^ Mullins and himself had just returned from Neepawa where they had discussed the

building of this road with the Hon. Mr. Murphy. They stated that Mr. Murphy had said that if I would write you requesting that this road be approved by you, as a relief project on the usual basis, that it would be built.

Mr. Peden requested that I give you the approximate mileage and the estimated cost of this work which is as follows:
Mileage, 76 miles.
Estimated cost, $6,000 to $10,000 per mile, depending upon width of road.
I would appreciate hearing from you at your earliest convenience.
Yours very truly,
W. R. Clubb,
Minister of Public Works and Labour.
Now no one asserts or has in this discussion asserted that Mr. Clubb was a supporter of the then government at Ottawa; no one has asserted that the Hon. Mr. Griffiths was a supporter of the government at Ottawa, and yet Mr. Griffiths, Senator Mullins and Mr. Peden, who was a supporter of the government, waited tin Mr. Clubb, as the letter I have just read, dated September 4, 1935 indicates.

Hon. W. A. Gordon,-
Under date of July 27, 1935, I wrote you with reference to the Piney highway and also under date of July 23 with reference to the Sprague-Morden road. Minister of Public Works and Labour, Winnipeg, Manitoba.
Reference your letters fourth instant Piney highway Sprague Morden road and Russell Clear Lake road. Yours very truly,
W. A. Gordon, Minister of Labour.
I propose now to read the order in council which authorized the agreement, and the agreement itself:

Certified to be a true copy of a minute of a meeting of the committee of the privy council, approved by His Excellency the Governor Gener-al on the 10th September, 1935.

-from the minister of labour submitting:
(1)	That parliament has enacted legislation which may be cited as the Relief Act, 1935;

He takes in a lot of territory.
"My experience in politics, based on a number of years," he asserted, "is, that the best way to get good roads in a province is to have an election every six months."
"If there is one great need in Canada," he continued, "it is the need for good roads. And apparently governments in power and the opposition candidates, knowing that the people want roads, certainly don't hesitate to provide them and the party in power start to build before elections. The reason I say that there should be an election every six months is that the people know that as soon as an election is over the majority of road projects stop too."
All in conformity with the letter which he sent to the leader of the opposition.

My correspondence with Mr. Bennett was confidential. Maybe I was inexperienced in having written but all know politicians. I at least was sincere."

"The provincial administration who had asked for roads had done so in political partisanship with the federal Liberal party and hoped the Conservative government would not go ahead. I deemed it good generalship to fight them with their own weapons.

This letter shows the rigid control of the federal department which had been exercised for some months before the minister made those statements. It reads: Dear Sir:
As you are aware a few weeks ago the dominion government proposed some very restrictive terms which had to be complied with in the administration of relief contributed to by the dominion.
The views of the municipalities were obtained and representations urging modifications were made to the dominion authorities. The honourable Minister of Labour for the dominion government decided to what extent the requests would be agreed to. Some of the suggestions were adopted, some were not.
A revised agreement has been received, and we are informed that the dominion government requires this agreement carried out effective from January 1, 1938, in order to qualify for dominion contribution towards relief.
In order to obtain the dominion assistance towards relief it is required that we approve of this agreement and return it. It has already been signed by the dominion authorities. A copy of the agreement is attached.
Under the terms of the agreement the province must undertake to see that the municipalities carry out the provisions of the agreement.
Attention is called to section in regard to earnings while off relief. Your municipality has been included as one of the places where this will be carried out. We shall be glad to have your suggestions as to the system which might be evolved for carrying out this arrangement.
Before we can put your January accounts through for payment it will be necessary for you to have a resolution of council forwarded to me, in which it is agreed that your municipality will carry out the terms of the agreement.
Will you kindly arrange to deal with this important matter as promptly as possible.

Among the terms of the agreement I find this, in the first part of section 6:
The province agrees to establish and maintain standards of eligibility for material aid in accordance with this agreement. . . .
Section 7 reads:
The province agreed that the maximum value of material aid (which is contributable to pursuant to this agreement) given to any head of a family or other individual, of itself, or together with any additional allowances or material aid made by the province and/or a municipality, shall be less than the normal earnings of an unskilled labourer in the district wherein the recipient resides, as averaged over the year proceeding the granting of aid with account taken of average loss of time; in determining said maximum for heads of families adjustment may be made for normal earnings of dependents of employable age and of proved employability.
I am informed by the city authorities that this in effect has led to a very low standard of relief. For instance this last clause I have just read has cut assistance to some families of ten persons to $70 a month, including clothing. Therefore it would seem as if this agreement, insisted upon by the dominion government, is made a prerequisite to the province receiving grants in aid of relief; and the province in turn is being forced to insist that the provisions should be carried out by the municipal authorities. This has resulted in a lowering of the standards that ordinarily prevail at least in my own city. Paragraph 9 of the agreement reads:
To remove from the minds of recipients of material aid the fear that in accepting such work as is available they may sacrifice the possibility of receiving said aid in the future when further need arises, and to ensure that seasonal workers shall make, out of their earnings, reasonable provision for seasonal employment, the province undertakes to require all cities and towns listed in schedule A to this agreement to provide each person in those jurisdictions who is ceasing to receive material aid during the term hereof, by reason of entering gainful occupation, a statement of the rate of material aid hitherto granted and a reasonable budget of expenditures for the individual or family while the breadwinner is in gainful occupation and to further require them to obtain a properly certified statement of earnings to be filled in and signed by employers of the applicant prior to his or her readmission for material aid benefits.
This means in effect that the standard of living is controlled for the man who has been in receipt of relief, even though he passes off relief. Talk about regimentation! We have heard from the other side of the house some very strong protests against anything that would look like regimentation. But, according to these arrangements, if a family has been on relief, the government pursues them

after they are off relief, insisting that they carry on their budgeting in a certain way. One can understand that if a family has been on relief for a considerable time, a good many household supplies may be short; they may need bedclothes and a score of things that they have not been able to purchase. Of my own city I can say this, that they have tried their best to meet the abnormal situation by treating the citizens as generously as possible. Let us take the case of an average labourer, a man who may be working for thirty cents an hour, a wage which is common in these days. If he worked fifty hours a week at thirty cents an hour he would earn $15 a week. That would be the salary for a full week, or a salary of approximately $60 a month. If he worked six months in the year, his earnings would be $480. If he happened to be the head of a large family, he could not receive in relief more than he had been earning on an average during the year, or the sum of only about $40 a month during the twelve month period. The father of six or eight children under those circumstances would be compelled to live on $40 a month, and that is where the hardship arises. That is where we say there has been interference on the part of the federal authorities in connection with the amount of relief granted to those who unfortunately have been compelled to become the recipents of public relief.
I believe the federal government ought not to have interfered in the scale of relief, when relief was being given as in the past. I know of very few instances where the amounts given could in any sense of the term be called high. Early in the month of April I placed on Hansard the amounts received in Winnipeg by way of relief. I forget the exact amount, but I know it was a very small one indeed. reading from the report of the national employment commission he referred to the necessity of having a relief scale sufficient to maintain health and decency. Does the minister believe that any family can maintain health and decency on the present relief scale?

I am quite right in saying that so far as the relief scales are concerned >they are determined by the provinces, subject to that maximum which I have described. I would remind the committee that the maximum is based upon the normal earnings of an unskilled labourer in the particular locality. The working out of the whole matter is left to the provincial government. If, in the opinion of the provincial government, a particular hardship is being worked, undoubtedly representations will be made to us. As I recall it, there has been always a certain amount of flexibility.

Does the minister think
that a standard of health and decency can be maintained with the normal earnings of an unskilled labourer? Would the minister adopt that scale for himself? If he would not adopt it, why accept it as a standard for others?

Apparently the government
now sheds responsibility because of having paid a lump sum. Representations have been made by certain cities asking that the federal government should take over the whole matter of relief. Relief will never be handled in a satisfactory manner until it is centralized-

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
Some time ago a lady called upon me. She had seven or eight children, and I understand her husband had been an inmate of an asylum. I believe she called on almost every member of the house. She had appealed to the local authorities, but the question of domicile had been raised. She was told that unless she returned to the province of Quebec she would not be able to obtain assistance. That seems to me a most stupid and unfair attitude to take. It should make no difference where a person resides. The fact that he is destitute should be sufficient reason for his receiving assistance. I do not know whether the minister is familiar with the case to which I am referring. This should not happen in the world's richest country.
I should also like to draw the attention of the minister to a matter in connection with the agreement entered into between the province of Alberta and the federal government.
I have not the agreement before me, but I understand the effect of it worked out in this way. Certain road work was carried on in one part of the province. There were a number of farmers in that locality who were not classified as destitute because they had equipment and horses. Most of them were actually worse off than if they were destitute, because they had had no crop for some years. Men were brought in from as far away as Calgary, a hundred miles away, to work in this locality. People in the immediate locality could not get employment under this agreement.

The control of employment lies with the province subject to the proviso that fifty per cent shall be taken from the relief rolls, or from those who are otherwise certified as being in needy circumstances. We have no control over the movement from one district to another, apart from the relief quota.

That is what I am dealing with right now. There were 100 men required on this work, and there were at least that many in that particular district who required work. Men were brought from Calgary to work. I discussed this matter with the provincial minister of public works, but he told me they could not do otherwise because it was on those terms that the money was obtained. To go into this question of relief would require hours. The whole system requires overhauling because it is a disgrace to this country. An investigation was held recently in the city of Ottawa and we saw spread across the pages of some of the local papers the statement that so many people on relief had radios and motor cars. I cannot
understand the mentality of a man or woman who would deny the right of a person who has been employed at some time and who has purchased a radio to have some enjoyment from that radio when forced to go on relief. Some people seem to think the minute a man goes on relief he must give up every comfort. If a man should get employment at low wages and work for three months, when he goes back on relief his relief allowance is based on what he earned. In other words, these people are not encouraged to find employment. When they do obtain employment their condition is no better than when they were on relief.
Surely we are not so devoid of ideas in this country that we cannot change this condition. There is plenty of work to do in this country and we should devise a scheme to do it. Is there any logical reason why it should not be done? Unfortunately this whole matter has assumed a certain permanency. It is no longer temporary in character. It has been with us for seven long years. While we may be able to measure the cost of relief in dollars and cents, we shall never be able to measure the mental anguish that has been caused by this stupid policy. This policy has retarded our industrial expansion and is possibly the greatest factor in bringing on our present-day depression. It has increased the mill rate in our municipalities and has made heavier the burden upon the taxpayers. As the right hon. leader of the opposition said in one of his excellent speeches, it is only an insurance against insurrection. Before this session ends, the government should give consideration to the abolition of relief, with the exception of relief to those who are classified as unemployables. Relief should not be necessary in the world's richest country.
I think it is time the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) got together to issue credit in terms of public need. That would be tne best answer to this problem. That would be the one way to get able-bodied men back to work. We are destroying the greatest asset possessed by this dominion. We are shrivelling up the initiative of the men of our country. Unfortunately, in party politics members sit back persistently and say nothing because they fear they may embarrass their party. Hon. members on the other side of the house should be bringing pressure to bear upon the government to do away with relief. It is a disgrace in the terms in which it is carried on at the present time. It is making slaves of men, and it has resulted in a reduction of wages all over the country.
Has the minister any information as to the number of men who have been laid off by the

I think the federal government should get together with the provinces and municipalities and devise a uniform relief scale as the first step necessary to be taken. If we recognize that relief must be continued for two years until we get an unemployment insurance scheme or there is a greater degree of employment in this country, there will be continued suffering on the part of our people until we devise a uniform scale of relief, and this question of domicile should be dealt with as one of the first and major problems. One of the great things about the unemployment insurance scheme in Great Britain is that a man residing, say, in the city of London can .move and take up his residence in Manchester and still be a beneficiary under the scheme. But here the limit of a man's activities in search of work is the distance he can walk, and that is one point that should be dealt with. If a man in Halifax happens to go to Vancouver and become destitute, if he can prove it, he should be a beneficiary of relief, and the fact that he has not resided in Vancouver for twelve months is a foolish reason for turning him. down.

I wish, to revert to the question of maximum relief and to clause 7 of the agreement between the provinces and the federal government. The minister must be aware of the fact that there have been men partly employed and even men fully employed who have been compelled to become recipients of public relief. I know instances of that kind in recent times, and if clause 7 is to be carried out according to the strict interpretation of its terms, the minister must realize the deplorable position in which cases of that kind must be. A man in that position would not earn more than $40 a month on an average, a totally inadequate sum as a basis of relief,

and, under the agreement, cases of that kind could not be dealt with in any special way at all. They would be compelled to be dealt with strictly according to the terms of the agreement; otherwise municipalities and provincial governments would run the risk of having the agreement cancelled and the federal grant stopped. I am wondering if the minister would not merely consider but try to get some understanding with the provinces for the overhauling of this clause of thr agreement to give some leeway to both provincial and municipal authorities so that they will not necessarily have to deal with the smaller family in the same way as the larger family seeking relief is dealt with.
Further, when you establish a scale of relief, its maximum tends to become the standard for all those in receipt of relief, and if a family of eight, two adults and six children, are compelled to live on $35 a month, that might readily determine the whole scale of relief to be granted in a particular area. That is something which ought to be seriously considered, and I am wondering whether the minister and his officials would not take into their serious consideration the necessity of revising that clause in the agreement to give the leeway I suggest to both the provinces and the municipalities.

Are the agreements between the federal government and the provinces of a hard and fast nature, or is there any method of making slight adjustments here and there in the agreement? I have reference particularly to the agreement with Alberta in connection with road work. I recall being at a place where a road gang was at work; they were doing very fine work, and the men were apparently happy to get the work. But the agreement evidently stipulated that a certain number employed on the work must be on relief, and some possibly could be employed who were not on relief. There were openings on this work for men who were on relief. Men and some horses were required to do certain work. This was noised to an adjoining munieipalitj' that had been very hard hit and had several families on relief, and it was suggested that they needed horses and one or two men to do this work. The horses happened to arrive when I was there, in charge of a young man from a family that was on relief. The father was an old man, and he did not feel that he could go over with the horses, do the road work himself, sleep in a tent and eat in a cookhouse, so he sent over his son who was living at home, a strong, young chap, but when he arrived he was told that it was impossible

Supply-Labour-Relief Commitments
for him to get work because he himself was not on relief. He was told he could not work in his father's place. I recall going to the engineer or some official appointed by the federal authorities, but he could do nothing about the matter. I went to the M1.A. for the constituency, but he could do nothing about the matter, and what, finally happened I do not know to this day. It does seem to me that there should be some method of making adjustments in these agreements, that the agreements themselves should be elastic enough to permit of slight adjustments being made. What are the possibilities along that line?

I can only say that in the agreement with Alberta covering joint works provision was made that fifty per cent should be taken from the relief rolls or from those who were in necessitous circumstances. There was provision for those who were unemployed but who were not on relief. As a matter of fact, that agreement with Alberta was not carried out in its strict terms. I do not know if that is what my hon. friend has in mind. At all events the administration of it has to be left to the provincial authorities subject to the approval of a dominion representative or a dominion inspector, as the case might be. There is a certain amount of latitude with respect to the employment clause, as I have indicated; but my hon. friend will also realize that much may be said in the direction of making the terms of the agreement strict, in order to prevent the possibility of abuse. If you make the agreement too loose, obviously it is open to abuse.
I might point out, Mr. Chairman, that actually we are dealing with a special item in the supplementary estimates respecting relief agreements with the provincial governments, and not with the item in the main estimates for relief. I do not want to press that point too strongly except that I should like to make some progress.
Is it not true that the federal government approves the various projects which the province may undertake?
Yes.

I realize that this discussion might not come under the item before us, but the discussion has been going on for some time, and I should just like to raise this point. The federal government stipulates that a certain percentage of those employed on these projects must be relief recipients or people in necessitous circumstances. Second, the federal government must approve the project. Suppose the federal government approves a project which requires 51952-251
trucks for graveling a highway; how many relief recipients would have trucks? It is not logical to expect them to have trucks, and the result is that when the province makes its claim on the dominion government for payment the dominion government says:	You
did not employ people on relief. But it knows that it was impossible to engage people on relief because they did not have the necessary equipment. I believe that situation has arisen in several cases in Alberta, particularly in the northern part of the province, and it puts the provincial government entirely at the mercy of the federal government.
The point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is this, that in the case of agreements of this kind being made with various provinces, I do not see any reason why some of these agreements or at least a standard agreement could not be embodied in the act authorizing the agreements, so that these things could be discussed in parliament. At the present time there is absolutely no way in which one can bring these things to the attention of the minister until the harm has been done. I suggest to him that if he would incorporate in his empowering act some standard agreement which he will put into effect with the provinces, we would then have an opportunity of knowing whether or not the thing was being properly handled from every point of view.

When this item was up for consideration before the house adjourned the night before last, I asked the minister what public works were being undertaken in British Columbia in which this government was interested and on which work might be available for the unemployed who are sitting

in the Vancouver post office and art gallery. I understood him to say that the two main projects were the Big Bend highway and the new highway from the United States boundary to New Westminster, and he also said that these men, along with certain other classes of unemployed, would be eligible for that work. Last week I understood him to say that summer training in the special forestry camps could be undertaken by the younger men among these unemployed. He said at that time that the forestry camps had not yet been opened, but I notice from the Vancouver press that the first training camps were opened about ten days ago. As for the transients who do not belong to British Columbia, I believe the government's attitude is that they must go back to their own provinces if they wish to get assistance at all. Has any move been made to offer these men work or to offer those who are eligible training in the forestry camps, or has any promise been made that there will be work or training for at least some of them? This is of great importance, and it might help to solve the difficulty if an offer or a promise of that kind were made. Has the government made any move in that direction?

I answered my hon. friend the other day with regard to the chief works that were in prospect in British Columbia. As he has said, one of these projects was the Big Bend highway, and the other is the new highway to be constructed from the international boundary to New Westminster. There are other works in addition to that-harbour works and public works of various kinds, as well as work which is now under way in connection with the expansion of national defences in that area. Those who are single and unemployed, presently in Vancouver, and who are at the same time resident in British Columbia, would be on the same footing as others who are single and unemployed and resident in that province, so far as employment in these works is concerned. I told my hon. friend that the other day, and I cannot go beyond that at the present time.

But the government has
in Vancouver a special representative, a Mr. Humphrey Mitchell, who has been there for weeks. Has any offer been made to these men that they may go on this work, or has any promise been made that within the next week or two they will be able to do so? May I have an answer to that question?

I believe a statement was issued by the minister of labour of British Columbia with respect to employment on

I have spoken about the
seriousness of the situation on two or three occasions, and I hesitate very much to place it before the house again, but I believe that the government and perhaps most members in this house do not realize how serious the situation is. For four weeks to-morrow there have been hundreds of men sitting in the Vancouver post office and art gallery. It is what might be called a sit-down strike.

We have been told that
a dozen times.

And you will be told it
again. The government is apparently carrying on a sit-down strike here. The net result is that Vancouver is being subjected to the most adverse kind of publicity possible. It is seriously affecting the tourist business, which means a great deal to the city. It is absolutely unfair to the citizens because they have to support the men, and there are threats of riots, there is always the fear of riots. In short, it is creating in the third city of Canada a spirit of hopelessness and the belief that there will be no action or leadership on the part of the government.
These men were cared for all winter by the dominion and the provincial governments in the regular forestry camps. They were let out, I believe, not all at once; the dismissals were staggered, which was a very good thing. But it was known, we warned the government weeks ago, that many men were losing their work in the logging camps of British Columbia and that it would be impossible to place these men in the logging camps as was done last summer. It was known that their funds would soon run out, that they would all congregate in Vancouver and that there was bound to be trouble. Yet nothing has been done; everyone is "just sitting." That situation is absolutely unfair to the people of Vancouver. Some action should be taken by the government without further delay. There is no excuse for this gap. The men were all out of the camps by the end of April, and yet the public works program does not start until July. There is a responsibility resting directly on this government; and all the more because its own commission, the Purvis commission, found that these men were the
charge of the federal government, recommended that all employables should be the charge of the federal government. Yet nothing is done.
If I might correct my hon. friend, if he will examine the text of the report he will find that is not quite what the commission recommended.

Well, it went about that far. The problem of the transient is the crux of the whole unemployment problem. How this or any federal government can say that transients coming from the prairies or Ontario or Quebec to British Columbia are the charge of the British Columbia government or of the people of Vancouver is beyond me. This unemployment is a national emergency. It is the problem of the national government. We have here another example of the spinelessness of this government; another case of "wait and see," just drifting along. Something should be done by the government about these men in the post office and the art gallery in Vancouver without further delay.

The Vancouver rotary club was recently addressed by the secretary of the chamber of commerce of Hongkong. He recited some of the horrors he had witnessed in China. Then he concluded his statement, according to the press reporrs, by saying he was reluctant to make any appeal for funds in Vancouver, because on entering the post office he had found that Canada had a refugee problem of her own, and he saw people camped on the floor of this public building under conditions which, considering the difference in the standard of living, were worse than those in the refugee camps in China.
The minister has said that if these men disperse, they will have advantages equal to those of other unemployed in other parts of British Columbia and the dominion. I am receiving reliable information that the training courses in forestry and placer mining now being opened are not available to these men; the quota has now been filled. Furthermore. I am reliably advised that these men are now barred from any work that may arise, by reason of their connection with this affair. And that action has been condoned by the representative of the federal Department of Labour in Vancouver. These men are being blacklisted and outlawed. I suggest to the minister that not only has this demonstration on the part of the men revealed a problem which he has not lifted a finger to deal with, but he has actually condoned through his representative a procedure which outlaws these men and is likely to be provocative of serious

disorder. The action of the minister or his representative must be explained. The minister's representative in Vancouver is responsible in large measure for provoking and continuing this extremely embarrassing situation.

Let me answer that at once. It is certainly not true that the representative of the Department of Labour of this government has had any authority, or to my knowledge has exercised any authority, such as that stated by my hon. friend. I indicated very clearly in my last telegram to Mr. Matts and the unemployed committee that so far as youth training projects or federal public works are concerned, these men on going to their own homes or their province of origin would be upon the same footing as others in a similar position; in other words, that they were not to be disqualified for such employment as is available. I have not altered that, it certainly applies to federal works, and so far as I am aware there has been no restriction as far as joint works are concerned. Of course, on joint works we can control employment only up to fifty per cent.

Is there any truth in the
statement that the department's representative, Mr. Mitchell I understand, in association with other officials in touch with the problem, has said that these men will not now get any work that is open; that he in conjunction with other officials has determined that.
If my hon. friend will be good enough to give me the authority for his statement, I shall look into it. I should be glad to receive it privately.

At relief camp No. 1, Vancouver post office, I am informed in a letter I received that the blankets and old coats and newspapers make such a stench in that building that it is no longer used as a public post office by those who have business to transact; that it is offensive to people to go there. I remember distinctly members of the present government when in opposition made very strong claims about sanitary conditions in relief camps, and we had officers of the Department of National Health take great care with respect to that. This relief camp No. 1 in Vancouver would seem to be in rather bad condition.

outstanding owing to Alberta which are being withheld by reason of some dispute as to whether the agreements have been lived up to either by the province or the federal government?

How long have negotiation? been going on between the dominion government and Alberta for the payment of that sum?
For something over a year I should say.
What is the condition which allegedly has been violated by Alberta, causing the present government to withhold those sums?

My hon. friend is not stating the position quite correctly. It is rather a case of Alberta having recognized that they were under obligation to make a refund. The particular clause of the agreement that was not carried out by the province related to the fifty per cent relief quota.
